english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO 1. This chapter deals with the characteristics of true and false teachers and disciples. It opens with the ‘great arising from Meru’ of the teachers of previous aeons At first sight it appears that this passage is independent of the rest of the chapter and has little to do with it, but that is not so. All major rites begin with the worship of the lineages of teachers and cannot be performed without knowing them. It supplies information that an initiate must know to qualify him to be a true teacher and hence is one of his characteristics. In the earliest period of the formation of the rites of the Kubjikā Tantras the worship of the first teachers was confined to those related to the emanations of the Bhairava’s forms, that is, the Five Siddhas. Subsequently, to these were added the Nine Nāthas who were originally the Bhairavas of the nine letters of Navātman, his seed-syllable mantra. The Sixty Teachers and One Hundred Teachers is a later addition that aims to sink the roots of the tradition firmly not just to earlier Ages (yuga) but also aeons (kalpa). A similar series of teachers, but with entirely different names, is found in the first chapter of what remains of the Kulakaulinīmata. The µīkā (MS K fl. 182b) in the course of its commentary on this chapter of the KuKauM reproduces the same list, which we need not do here. Our text lists one hundred teachers, corresponding to as many years distributed through the four Ages (yuga). The KuKauM refers to just sixty teachers called the Sixty Years (saˆvatsara or abda) named after the years in which they received the goddess’s grace (yasya yasya yasmin yasmin saˆvatsare ‘nugraho [k kh: -haˆ] jātaƒ [k kh: jātaˆ] sa [k kh: te] ca saˆvatsaraƒ | µ ibid.). Belonging to the three lineages, they are closely related (bhratrvarga) and are said to have lived at the end of the aeon (kalpa) in the Deccan (dakniSāpatha) (san˜yabdās te samākhyātāƒ kalpānte dakniSāpathe KuKauM 1/23cd). The text stresses that it is essential to know the correct order of seniority of these teachers and those of one’s own lineage (svoli). Accessible only to initiates of that lineage, this knowledge is a sign that they belong to it. Thus, those who possess it may freely participate in the rites and dine together. 2. Cf. above 14/4-5.

The equivalent imperative forms are गृह्णीयात् and गृह्णीत. This deviant form occurs only here in the KuKh, but it appears not less than six times in the commentary on the SSS (MS Kh folios 18a, 186b, 210a, 243a, 247a and in folio 80a as निग्राहयेत्) and in the T. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE 1. After the brief digression in the previous chapter, in this one we return to the theme of chapter thirty-one, namely, initiation. This chapter is called ‘concerning the Initiation with Seed’ The distinction between initiation ‘with seed’ and ‘without seed’ is defined concisely by the CMSS as follows: The initiation by mantra `with seed' involves offerings to the fire (hutā) with clarified butter, cooked rice and sesame seed. Kaulikī initiation is `without seed' and consists of the piercing (vedha) (of the inner centres). mantradīknā sabījā ca ājyānnaiƒ [k, kh, g: ājyānna; gh: ājyanna] satilair hutā [k: latilai hutaˆ; kh: laˆtilair hutam; g: latilair hutam; gh: latilaihutaˆ] || nirbījā [k g: nibījā; gh: -ja] kaulikī dīknā [g: dīknyā] vedhanātmasvarūpataƒ [sarve: vedhamātma-] | CMSS 3/56cd-57ab Our text similarly refers to the first kind of initiation as one that involves offerings to the fire (hotrīdīknā). This is defined as a Tāntrika initiation and contrasted with the other which is a Kaula initiation (33/19cd-20). The second kind ‘without seed’ is taught first (up to 33/53). The other kind — ‘with seed’ — is the subject of the rest of the chapter which is drawn from chapter nine (verses 1 to 244) of the Tantrasadbhāva. The first type of initiation (‘with seed’) is by means of the Principles (tattvadīknā), that is, by means of the Six Paths (naÆadhvan). This is explained from line 53cd to the end of the chapter, which is mostly all drawn from chapter nine of the Tantrasadbhāva. The other (‘without seed’) is Initiation by Piercing, which is not based on the Six Paths. It is treated first in a passage (from the beginning of the chapter to line 53ab) that may be either drawn from a different source or, quite possibly, is an original part of the text of the KuKh. 2. Initiation is generally understood in all Tantric traditions to be a means to gain both worldly benefits (bhoga) and liberation. Here, the latter is represented as Yoga, which is, as the word literally means, ‘union’. It is the liberating union of the individual soul with the Supreme Principle. This Yoga is brought about by the forms of initiation that take place by piercing (vedha) the inner centres of the subtle body (33/21) with the energies and aspects of the Command. Thus it is called the Yoga of the Command. See below 33/17-18ab and above, 31/88cd-89. 3. It appears that a part of the text in which the remaining states are listed has been lost. 4. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE 74 54. The Three Principles are: 1) Vidyātattva that includes the 24 principles (tattva) from Earth to Prakrti. 2) Ātmatattva that includes the eleven principles from the Person (puruna) to Śakti. 3) Śivatattva that includes just Śiva. 55. TS (9/195cd): O fair lady, the (Path of the) Worlds and the rest should be fashioned by the most excellent knowers of the scriptures. bhuvanādyā varārohe kartavyā śāstravittamaiƒ || 56. The text is corrupt here. All the MSs read: karSādim āditaƒ krtvā. I have emended to kalādi- which agrees with the reading in the TS but perhaps kālādi- would be better as the worlds are commonly said to be fifty ranging from Kālāgni to Śiva (see 2/41 and note). However, this emendation may also be correct as the first Energy (kalā) does correspond to the element Earth. 57. TS (9/199d): ‘. . . in accord with the desired goal (kāmyānurūpataƒ).’ 58. Karma is defined as consisting of Dharma and Adharma. Although described here as two fetters (see below 33/173-174), we should understand them to be two aspects of the one fetter which is Karma (see above, 13/80cd-81). 59. The basic impurity — āSavamala — is generically called sahajamala, which means both ‘innate impurity’ and ‘impurity born at the same time (as the fettered soul)’. 60. TS: ‘,,, there is no liberation there for anybody’. 61. See above, note to 33/162. 62. See above, note to 13/54 and TĀ 1/43-4. 63. See above, 31/32cd-35ab, 33/46-47 and notes.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-FOUR 1. The text here may be implying that renouncers who 'live off others' are in an inferior state to the householder. But the following provisor may also be taken to refer to those renouncers whose minds, despite their condition, are still ‘smitten with attachment’. It also applies, of course, to householders in the same state of attachment. 2. Cf. below 34/97-8ab. 3. The image of the deity is usually on the right side of the Krama, which in this case is in the fire pit. 4. The triangle 'above' the altar is the fire pit. Thus the hexagonal altar with its triangular pit reproduces in three dimensions the core of the goddess's maSÆala in which she burns, as in the pit, as the VaÆavā fire along with her consort, Navātman. 5. This is the length of the human body. 6. Concerning the six limbs of the goddess’s Vidyā, see above 11/14 ff.. 7. In this list of thirteen purifications of the sacrificial hearth ‘proknaSa’ appears twice. Apparently, the two are different kinds of ‘washing’. The first is done at the beginning and the second is the penultimate purification that is coupled with an invocation of the deity and followed by the drying of the hearth and the area around it. 8. According to the SKh (MS G fl. 40a) Aghorāstra is: AI¤ HRAU¤ [K: HRĀ¤] HRĀ¤ HRAÖ AGHORĀSTRĀYA K±AÖ Aghorāstra is uttered first to make a place for the goddess to sit. After that comes the goddess embodied in her two seed-syllables, AI¤ and HSKHPHRE¤. 9. The Scalpel of Knowledge (jñānaśalāka) is probably meant here. This is the syllable HSKHPHRE¤. See note to 5/35-6. 10. The King of Weapons (astrarāja) is the Ko‰kaSa Weapon (ko‰kaSāstra). This is the sixth of the Kubjikā’s six limbs (naÆa‰ga). It is (SKh MS G fl. 43b): AI¤ HRĪ¤ ŚRĪ¤ KHPHRE¤ HSAUÖ KI¦I KI¦I VICCE KO¥KA¦ĀYAI [KH: KO¤KA¦ĀVVĀYAI] ASTRĀYA AI¤ An extended, elaborated form is extracted in YKh (1) (1/264cd-274ab) consisting of. 42 syllables. It is as follows: KI¦I x 2 VICCE x 3 KHI¦I KHI¦I x 4 KO¥KA¦ĀVVĀYAI ASTRĀYA x 2 HU¤ PHAµ x 2 HU¤

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-FOUR 90 66. Kubjeśī is represented by her syllable AI¤. 67. Concerning bali offerings see above 11/33cd-34ab. 68. The fire sacrifice of YKh (1) enjoins that the two spoons undergo a series of purifications, which it lists as follows: Next I will tell (you) about the big and little spoons, according to the manner of worship. The rites are those of bringing the spoons, looking (at them), sprinkling, grasping (them), heating (them), placing them facing each other, the deposition of the Three Principles in one, the tying of the thread by the union of Śiva and Śakti, cleaning, purification, displaying the gesture and the deposition of the energies. (Thus) you have been told about the purifications (saˆskāra) of the big and little spoon. They should be worshipped with Śikhārāja, Caitanya and the PraSava. Having done so, pick them up with the left hand. ataƒ parataraˆ [k, kh: paraˆ-; gh: pa * -] vaknye [k, kh: vakne] śruk [kh: śrukra] śruvaˆ [k, kh, gh: śruve] ca yathārcanam [gh: -rcaˆrna || śrukśruvānayanaˆ [kh, gh: śrukraśruvā-] caiva nirīknaSaˆ proknaSaˆ tathā | grahaSaˆ tāpanaˆ [k, kh, gh: pratāpanaˆ] caiva sanmukhīkaraSaˆ tathā || tattvatrayaikavinyāsaˆ [k, kh, gh: tatvatrayekavinyāsaˆ] sūtrabandhanam eva ca | śivaśaktisamāyogānmārjjanaˆ śodhanaˆ tathā || mudrāsaˆdarśanaˆ cānyaˆ [k, kh, gh: cānya] kalānyāsaˆ tathaiva ca | śrukśruvasya [k, kh, gh: śruknūstuvasā] ca saˆskārāƒ [k, kh, gh: -rā] kathitās te varānane [k, kh: -nā] || śikhārājena vinyāsaˆ caitanyena tathaiva ca | praSavaiś ca tataƒ pūjya vāmahastena grhnayet || YKh (1) 1/234cd-238 69. 'Going' is the forward direction. 'Coming' is the reverse. The mantra is repeated counting the beads first forward up to the main bead, called Meru and then backwards back to the Meru. See note to 3/122cd-3ab. 70. Cf. above, 11/58. 71. Apāmārga = Achyranthes Aspera. Śārdūla = Plumbago Zeylanica. Somarājī = Vernonia Anthelminthica. Pippala = Ficus Religiosa (the Peepal tree). Īśvara is the name of several plants. Brahmā = Clerodendrum Siphonantus. Jīmuta = Luffa Foetida and Meghavāhana = Cyperius Rotundus. 72. No mention is made of any sacrificial fee in the case of the regular rite, presumably because the householder does it himself.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-FIVE 1. Perhaps by Gahvara is meant the Kulagahvaratantra which is the source of KuKh 31/11cd-26a. Or else ‘Gahvara’ may be a category of Tantras. 2. See note to 24/3cd-4. 3. Cf. above, 35/10 where it is clear that these three levels correspond to the sides of the goddess's Triangle. 4. See intro. vol. 1, 24 concerning the identity of KuSÆalinī as Nāsāśakti — the ‘energy of the nose’. 5. Cf. 35/38. 6. These are the Six Yoginīs — Õākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī with Yākinī as the seventh (see below 63/16-23ab). They constitute a well known group called Yoginīna˜ka or Õādina˜ka (see 44/28-31 and note). Externally they are worshipped in the corners of the hexagram within the maSÆala with Yākinī in the centre. Here they are projected into the Six Wheels in the subtle body. In the later representations of these Wheels there presence within them is one of their standard features. However, this is not the case in the Kubjikā Tantras, although, as in this case, the link is made. The link is justified because they share a common ‘foundation’. This is the hexagram, into the corners of which the Six Wheels, like the Six Yoginīs, are projected. See, chapter sixty-three which is dedicated to them. 7. The ‘parigraha’ is the ‘enclosure’ formed by the sides of the goddess’s triangle. See chapter 7, note 86. 8. The Wheels, in this context, are related to the sacred seats from which emanate the teachings and the creative energy of the goddess. They are described in the descending order, which is that of emanation (srnti). Below 35/48 ff. they are described in the ascending order. The sequence there ends with the Triangle that contains the sacred seats and is the condition of the goddess without form. In this case the sacred seats are positioned in the hexagram that emanates out of the central upper triangle. In this context the Island of the Moon is the Point in the centre (cf. 35/66 and note) although normally it is the Triangle. The Command is located in the Point above the Half Moon (35/66). 9. ‘Half of Half of Ha’ (hakārārdhārdha) is the Point. See intro. vol. 1, p. 352. 10. OÆÆiyāna is in Point in the centre of the Triangle. Directly below it is the Half Moon. The former is the Full Moon and the latter the New Moon. Perhaps the Fire of Time is the energy of the New Moon. The nectarine lunar energy of the goddess flows down from there through SunumSā into the uvula at the back of the throat in the 'cavity of the palate'. See note to 3/102. Collectively these three form the ‘supreme seat’. This is Oˆkāra / OÆÆiyāSa. Normally these are two names for the same seat but here they are distinguished. Clearly, the Command of Ritual Observance (anun˜hājñā) is another name for the Command of NirvāSa (nirvāSājñā). 2. karSāt karSagataˆ literally `from ear to ear'. 3. Cf. the VainSava’s devotee’s state in note 25 of chapter 31 above. 4. Concerning Vrknanātha see above 2/29-30ab. 5. Cf. AS 20/16cd-20ab quoted in note to 27/20-21. 6a. The Wheels are also described in 3/103cd ff., 25/5 ff. and 35/35cd ff.. 6b. Diagram 4. The Wheel of the Foundation Fire The Flame The Wheel of Fire Moon Sun 7. Concerning the signs of attainment, see above notes to 33/47-49. 8. The stick of the vital breath, also called the Stick of Energy, is the flow of inhalation and exhalation. (See below 36/59; 36/82cd-83ab). Mahāmudrā is one of five gestures that make energy move through the body (śakticālanamudrā) described in the Goraknaśataka. Although this is a later text and not a Tantra, it contains much that has been carried over from earlier Tantric traditions that have been lost. The Goraknaśataka explains: The purification of the collection of the channels (of the breath) (nāÆī) (that takes place by) the motion of both the Moon (of exhalation) and the Sun of (inhalation) along with the drying up of the liquids (rasa) (in of the body) is called the Great Gesture (mahāmudrā). english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-SIX 115 fall (even if he) is embraced by a passionate woman. As long as the Drop remains in the body there is no fear of death. As long as (the yogi maintains his) practice of (this) the Gesture of the Sky, the Drop does not move. (But) even if the Drop (happens) to reach the Fire (in the Yoni), it moves up arrested by the energy and checked by the Gesture of the Yoni. GS 64-70 translation (with modifications) by Briggs (1973: 297-298); see also A.K. Banerjea: 186-187. 22. These five states are arranged in a sequence (3/92cd-93ab). They are states the deity assumes (3/95cd-96) and are gathered together within him in the Stable Place, that is, the Wheel of the Command (36/95-96) where he resides in this fivefold form. In the following passage they mark the phases in the ascent and transformations of his energy, Raudrī as she moves through the subtle body. 23. In the Pāśupata system, the Stable Place was the highest of the series of worlds through which the observer of the Pāśupata Vow inwardly ascended. Here, some centuries later, its eminant status has been preserved and extended. Now, instead of Rudra, his energy stands supreme — Rudraśakti — who was identified in the early Trika with the Supreme Goddess and is here identified with Kubjikā. 24. The yogi is in the Wheel of the Foundation. To his left and right are the Sun and Moon, the two breaths, coursing through IÆā and Pi‰galā. Here he experiences the emergence of Raudrī’s energy, that is, KuSÆalinī, rising up through the central channel of SunumSā where the other two channels meet. 25. As Raudrī rises she passes through the five states. Initially she is pure Energy. Splitting it apart she emerges out of it as Light. When she emerges out of the Void of the Cavity of Form at the base of SunumSā she becomes Sound. When she reaches the palate she becomes the Point. Finally she assumes her state as pure Bliss in the Place of the Command, the Stable Place. Initially fierce when she emerged from the one Energy, she becomes peaceful in the Wheel of Tranquillity. 26. See above 36/88cd-89. 27. Ā stands for Ājñā, the Command in which the goddess is ‘established' (cf. 38/16). Thus the god is in the goddess, just as the goddess is within the god. 28. Note that only thirty-one deities are listed here not thirty-two. Moreover the first entry is Śrīnatha whereas all the rest are goddesses. It seems that a line or two of the text has been lost. The figure thirty-two suggests that these deities correspond to the syllables of the goddess’s Vidyā. Indeed, a good number are names of Kubjikā. 29. VaruSa is the guardian of the western quarter. Thus VaruSa's House is that of the Western Tradition. See below, 48/3. Also Ykh (1) (4/299d): śrīkramaˆ vāruSaˆ grham. Quoted above in note to 30/164-166ab. 30. Cf. above 36/81cd-82ab. 31. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-SEVEN Some lines and verses in this passage are also found in a passage in the ±SS (41/11-63) dealing with the same subject. These have been collated with the Sanskrit text and signalled as we go along in the notes to the translation. 3. Cf. 48/54. The Command operates for one who observes (the Rule). Without observing the Rule in this way, (the initiate has) no power (sāmarthya) and so, without power, (he does not experience) the plane of Stillness (nirācāra). Therefore without observing the Rule, the initiate falls and, degraded (bhran˜a), is destroyed. 6. Concerning how the scripture should be worshipped, see above note to 30/32. 1. The passage from 37/2cd to the end of this chapter is repeated in all the MSs after 47/28 where, as here, it runs to the end of the chapter. In chapter 47, this passage appears after a description of the initiation and naming ceremony of the neophite. This is indeed when the Rules that the initiate should observe are normally taught to him in the most common and basic form of the Śaiva rites of initiation. But this passage is not out of place here, coming as it does just after an exposition of the Kaula rites of initiation. Note that both this chapter and chapter 47 are called ‘the Practice of the Rule’. Thus it appears that the passage originally existed as an independent chapter to which additions were made to make it fit in these two places possibly by two separate redactors, the second of which failed to notice the repetition. 2. Cf. 44/53-63ab. 4. Similarly, the µīkā (fl. 80b) admonishes: yaƒ pālayet tasyājñā saˆpravartate | evaˆ samayapālena [k kh: + na] vinā sāmarthyaˆ na bhavati tasmāt sāmarthyena vinā nirācārapadaˆ na bhavati | tasmāt samayapālanena vinā patati [k kh: pa˜hyati] dīknitas tathā sa [kh: saƒ] bhran˜o [k kh: bhran˜a] nan˜aƒ | 5. The drawing and worship of the GurumaSÆala and the KramamaSÆala is taught in chapter 48. See also above 11/24b-53 where the KramamaSÆala is described. 7. KuKh 37/8cd-9ab = ±SS 41/32cd-33ab. One should first worship the book in a secluded, solitary place and then listen to the Kula scripture along with the (oral) teaching. Once heard the meaning of the teaching of the scripture in one's own Kula or in another, one should worship one's own Kulakrama on a mirror or auspicious seat (bhadrapī˜ha) and the excellent teacher who playfully saves from the terrible world of transmigration.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-EIGHT 1. This verse is a variant of the first verse of the Root Sūtra with which chapters 26 and 42 begin. The rest of this version of the sūtra develops in its own way. For an explanation of this verse see notes to 26/3. 2. The seat Tisra is the Half Moon, which symbolizes the New Moon. This is the ‘forehead’ of the syllable AI¤. Above that is the Point which symbolizes the Full Moon and is the location of the sacred seat of the Moon. Above the Point is the Wheel of the Mothers. This is the location of Ko‰kaSa. In many cases Ko‰kaSa replaces Candrapī˜ha, but here it is presented independently. Although not counted as a separate seat it is accorded a special, privileged status as the embodiment of the Wheel of the Mothers. This is said to be ‘above’. Elsewhere we have seen that the Circle of Mothers (mātrmaSÆala) is below Kāmarūpa (see intro. vol. 1, p. 109). Here it is ‘above’ which may possibly mean ‘surrounding’. The three encompassing rings usually represent the lights of the Sun, the Moon and Fire. 3. Cf. 26/4. 4. The six groups of six lisited here are the six Siddhas and the six Goddess along with the Six Wheels in which they reside. There are also six trees, creepers and seals. 5. Notice here how groups of six operate together with triads. The six are projected and worshipped in the corners of the hexagram that surrounds the triangle in the centre. The corners of the triangle are the locations of the triads. As the seat of the main deities, the centre differs from what surrounds it and so does not form part of a tetrad or group of seven. 6. The Aggregate of Letters are arranged in rows along the sides of the central Triangle in the manner described in chapter seven (8-16ab). The ‘sixfold process of differentiation’ is represented by the surrounding hexagram. 7. The One Verse is, presumably, the Single Syllable Vidyā HSKHPHRE¤, which is also called the Twelve Verses. Six of the ‘verses’ are the audible letters. The other six are the six energies of Sound above it (see 9/3cd ff.). The ‘three’ in the middle with the two groups of six, are, I suppose, the triads that make up the sides of the Triangle that surrounds the One Verse (made of six plus six parts). 8. The goddess is Mudrā who is in the centre of the Triangle, here called the 'triple wheel'. Kulīśa is the Point in the centre, the Divine Li‰ga whose threefold face is the Triangle. The goddess is also identified with the Divine Li‰ga (26/5). The One Verse is the syllable of the goddess, HSKHPHRE¤. The Lord is Navātman, HSK±MLVRYŪ¤ and is the Tamarind Tree. Below (in 38/8) he is identified with the Kadamba Tree. He is within Kula and Akula with which the goddess is identified (38/9). Below we find a reference to the 'Kula of six sheaths'

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-EIGHT 146 consonance in the Triangle of the Void (see 7/13 ff.; 14/61-62ab and also 40/132- 133) as three aspects of the Transmental. This is the energy of the Yoni, which in the Root Sūtra is accordingly said to be 'conjoined to the dynamism of the Three Paths' (tripathagatiyutā) (26/3a). So we read in the CMSS (quoted in comm. on TĀ 3/94cd-95ab): The Triangle is said to be the Yoni (bhaga). It is the secret Circle in the Sky. (Its) corners are will, knowledge and action. In the centre of it is the Transmission of the (goddess) Ciñcinī. 56. When the breaths move, transported by KuSÆalinī the vital force that animates them, she sleeps, coiled in the circular motion of the breath. But when the movement is fixed in the centre at ‘midnight’, she awakens and moves in the night when there is neither Sun nor Moon, wandering through the sacred sites of the Wheels up and out into the upper Triangle.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE 1. The texts regularly refer to the core of the maSÆala as a triangle (trikoSa), which is how it is drawn in two dimensions. However, it would be more accurate to think of it as a pyramid with a triangular base This is how we should understand the Stone to be. The Peak of the Stone is the apex of the pyramid which, drawn in two dimensions, is represented by a point in the centre of a triangle. 2a. Kulākula is the union of Śiva and Śakti (39/42). It is represented by the straight horizontal line at the top of the downward facing Triangle. Beyond it is the transcendental Candrikā Kula. Candrikā is the New Moon from which the sixteen energies of the Moon are emitted (see above 3/44). It is above the Triangle in the transcendent, which is the plane of the Skyfarer into which transcendental Śiva merges (39/43). 2b. 5. The Moonlight of the Void Jyen˜hā Kulākula Jālandhara Jyen˜hā K±a A PūrSagiri Vāmā Ma Ka Vāmā Kula Raudrī Akula Bha Ö Raudrī Kāmarūpa MaSipura Anāhata Svādhin˜hāna Viśuddhi Ādhāracakra Ājñācakra OÆÆiyāna

sanskrit: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE 157 3. In MS Jh we find the variant saṭkona - ‘six corners' for saṭkośa - ‘six sheaths'. The six 'sheaths' are the corners of the hexagram into which the Six Wheels are projected. Collectively this is called Kaula because it is derived from Kula, the triangle in the centre. One of the reasons the teachings of the Kubjikā Tantras are called 'Kulakaula' is because they are extensively concerned with these figures and their contents. The Six Wheels are, as in the previous verse, commonly called the ‘six parts'. They originate from the corners of the hexagram, the Kula of six sheaths. In the centre of the hexagram, the sphere of Kula, is the triangle, the Kula of the Heart. 4. Cf. 38/14-15ab. 5. The form of the letter Tha is a small circle. This is the 'ball' i.e. the Point which boundless, encompasses Emptiness full of all the energies. See below, 39/83cd-84 also 39/147. , - 6. The lunar asterism Rohini is called Sakaṭāhvā – the Cart. The Cart is the 'Cavity', that is, the Void of the Triangle surrounded by the three qualities of Nature that issue from it represented by the corners of the Triangle (39/35cd-36). The Half Cart is Bhairava, the Lord of Light (39/29cd-30ab), the male counterpart represented by the crescent Moon above the Point in the centre. Diagram 6. The Cart and the Half Cart of Bhairava Vāmā Jyestha Supreme Light • Energy Raudrī Bhairava Half Cart ठ ho Ball
english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE 158 7. The Supreme Energy is the threefold Yoni. It is on Bhairava’s head, immersed in his Light. This is another representation of self-perpetuation. The Point is in the centre of Yoni. This generates the Half Moon which generates the Yoni in the centre of which is the Point and so on ad infinitum. Thus Bhairava (the Half Moon) arises within the Yoni and the Yoni arises within Bhairava’s light. 8. Raudrī emerges from Vāmā and Jyen˜hā and yet she is all three. The centre contains the polarities, even as it emerges from them and generates them. The centre cannot be a centre without something to the right and the left. ‘Right’ and ‘left’ could not exist without the centre in relation to which they are to the right and to the left. Thus the Yoni generated through the self-perpetuating dynamism of the vertical process regenerates itself perpetually within it through the horizontal process. This is the dynamism of reality at its highest ‘extreme limit’. The Yoni immersed in the Light of Bhairava is pervaded and encompassed by him, even as the Yoni envelops and pervades Bhairava who is in the very core of the Yoni. 9. There are two kinds of Māyā. One that is binding which is ‘stained’ with ignorance and impurity. The other that is liberating and stainless. 10. The term mekhalā., which literally means ‘girdle’, normally denotes a circular enclosure that demarcates the periphery around the maSÆala. There may be more than one. In this case, it denotes the hexagram around the central triangle of the maSÆala. Doubled, this forms two triangles, one facing up and the other down. Thus, the Triangle is both the container and the contained. 11. This also a name of the constellation BharaSī. Concerning this etymology of the name Bhairava, see chapter one, note 85 and cf. 13/77cd-78. 12. After describing the surrounding Yoni, the Tantra goes on to talk about the Centre. This is where Bhairava resides within his energy, the power of bliss (1/1), just as she resides within him. He is bliss and she is the power of his bliss that makes him blissful. He is the body of bliss described in this case as the Krama. She is the energy, the vital force of his body — the command. 13. Concerning the Bliss of Stillness, see intro. vol. 1, p. 101 ff.. 14. This god is Pi‰gala Bhairava (39/41). One Kula is that of the manifest goddess who displays her qualities in the three seats in the corners of the female Triangle where they are in the balanced unmanifest (avyakta) state that precedes emanation. The other Kula is Bhairava, her consort in the centre. He is the manifest aspect the entire Body of Navātman that contains in potential form all the energies of the letters and their outer counterparts right down to the gross elements. Both are Void. United one with the other, they are Emptiness within Emptiness.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE 166 68. Pārameśvara is one of the names of the MBT. See intro. vol 3, p. 77. 69. To the right are the Yoginīs listed here. It appears that two Yoginīs are missing in this list. 1) Õakinī — Õakā + Raktodarā, 2) Rākinī — Rakā + Karālā and Lambodarā, 3) Lākinī — Lakā + Kumbhā and Bhagodarā 4) Kākinī — Kakā + Krśodarā; 5) Śākinī — Śakā + Yaknodarā and Ghorā, 6) Hākinī — Hakā + Raknodarā and Kulā Concerning the Hexad of Restraint and its varieties see chapter 63 which is dedicated to it. 71. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY 1. This chapter roughly corresponds to TS 1/11-321 and AS 20/190ab with which it has been collated. We are fortunate that MSs of the Tantrasadbhāva survive (see bibliography). In the transition from the source, the text has been subjected to alteration by the redactor first and then to further corruptions by scribes. Lacunae and additions add to the difficulty of understanding this chapter and the one that follows, which is drawn from the second half of the first chapter of the TS. Accordingly, to aid our understanding of these chapters, the corresponding text of the TS, when it differs significantly, and the omissions from it have been translated in the notes as we go along. Verses in the TS, omitted here, complete the context. Lines and words that coincide with the text of the KuKh are in bold face: O Rudra, I have heard the Veda, the secret as it truly is concerning what is kept concealed. O lord of the gods, the paths of the left and the right and the many Yāmalas, the Siddhāntas, in (their) ten and eighteen divisions with the part (of the scriptures) consisting of thousands of billions (of verses) and the thousands of millions of many kinds. Two sūtras have come forth in the great sūtra, that is, the root Tantra, the Siddhayogeśvarītantra that extends for a hundred million (śatako˜i) (verses). I have learnt one of these Tantras that has come forth from the Ocean of the Yoni (but) I have not heard, and wish to hear, the most excellent Tantrasadbhāva. The practice (caryā) of Tantra, ritual (kriyā), knowledge and Yoga are of many kinds. śrutaˆ [k, kh, g: śrutvā] vedaˆ [k, kh, g: veda] mayā rudra [k: rudrā; kh: tantrā; g: *?drā] rahasyaˆ gūÆhagocaram [k, kh: -gocarāƒ; g: ?] | vāmadakniSamārgāś [g: * *?dakniSa-] ca yāmalās tu anekadhā || siddhāntāś ca sureśāna daśān˜ādaśabhedataƒ | laknako˜ivibhāgena ko˜ayas tu anekadhā || siddhayogeśvarītantre śatako˜ipravistare | mūlatantre mahāsūtre sūtradvayavinirgatam [g: dā-] || na śrutaˆ śrotum icchāmi tantrasadbhāvam uttamam || tantraikaˆ] tu mayā [kh: mahā] jñātaˆ [kh: jñānaˆ] yonyārSavasamudbhavam [kh: yonyārSava * * * *] | tantracaryā kriyā jñānaˆ yogaś cāpi anekadhā | TS 1/11-15ab 2. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-ONE 1. AS and TS: The mind is always fickle (cañcala), without foundation and beyond the senses. 2. TS (1/327cd): Having abandoned the sense of ‘this is mine, everywhere one should reflect that: `I am not'. mamatvaˆ tyajya sarvatra nāham asmīti [g: nāntamasmīti] bhāvayet || 3. AS and TS: attain. 4. The TS (1/330) adds: Desire and aversion, pleasure and pain, detachment and attachment — as long as these are not abandoned how can he make progress? icchā [g: ?] dvenaƒ [k, kh: dvena; g: ?] sukhaˆ [g: ?] duƒkhaˆ [g: ?] virāgaś ca parigrahaƒ [k: virāgo mānavā tathā; kh: virāgo jñanavā tathā; g: virāgo jñānavā tathā] | yāvad ete [kh: etain] na mucyeta tāvat tasya kuto gatiƒ || 5. TS: Dragged back by the goad of ego fall (back) into the ocean of fettered existence. 6. TS: Having abandoned all longing he is said to be one who is free of longing. 7. AS and TS (1/337ab): Perceiving oneness (he realizes) ‘I am not, nor is there anybody else’. nāham asmi na cānyo ‘sti ekatvam anupaśyataƒ | 8. AS and TS (1/338-339ab) read instead of this verse: He who sees (reality) as it truly is (tattvena) and is established in the savour of oneness (samarasarasa) (perceives) the oneness (samatva) in all existing things (viewing) iron, stone and gold as the same. Thus he attains that state of equality and is said to be one who remains (always the) same (nirvikārin). paśyate yas tu tattvena samarasarase [k, kh, g: -rasorasaˆ] sthitaƒ [k: sthitaˆ] | samatvaˆ [kh: samatva] sarvabhūtenu samalon˜āśmakāñcanam || tena tatsamatāˆ [k, g: taˆ samatāˆ; kh: tatsamatā] yāti [k, g: yānti] nirvikārī sa ucyate [g: suducyate] | 9. AS and TS (1/339cd-340ab): He is free of thought constructs, is undefineable, beyond (any) means of knowledge and supreme. Thus there is no means (karaSa) (to attain that reality) which, established in its own essential nature, is its own characterizing mark (svalaknana).

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-ONE 242 (First) these (liberated souls) possess the pervasion of the Self and, beyond that, the pervasion of Śiva. (Although) they are free of all limiting adjuncts, due to the residual state (śenabhāva) of the fetters (that thus continue to exist) they have not know the supreme principle and so Śiva’s state is (merely) imagined by them. These Śaivas are not teachers of the Self. They do not reach Śiva’s plane. They reach the condition of the Self, (their) soul attached (rañjita) to the principle of the Self. Those who worship (deities) with forms having imagined (their) deities (to be such), (merely) attain their plane. They are not really liberated. Therefore, having abandoning everything one should worship (the reality which is) ‘established in the innate nature’ (svabhāvastha). english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-TWO 1. This chapter begins with the third and last version of the Root Sūtra (mūlasūtra) found in the KuKh. The other two are in chapters 26 and 38. Mukundarāja comments on the version in chapter 26 (see, note to 26/2). This version of the Root Sūtra contains little not found in the other two versions to which the reader is referred for an explanation. After the Root Sūtra, two other sūtras follow. They are the Sūtra of Action (kriyāsūtra) and the Sūtra of Emanation (srntikramasūtra). Mukundarāja’s brief commentary on these two sūtras is supplied in the notes. 2. Instead of ‘and fills the universe (pūrita)’ CMSS says: ‘Kāmarūpa is in the front of that (Yoni).’ 3. The Ciñcinīmatasārasamuccaya begins with a verse praising Śrīnātha (see note 22 of chapter 46) who descends into the world onto the Island of the Moon which is in the midst of the Ocean of Consciousness in the End of the Twelve. This is followed by one dedicated to the goddess and a third which extolls the essential practice the CMSS teaches, which is participation in her passionate and sacred love sport with the god. Here they are: I salute the venerable Kukārā of the tradition of the Western Tradition who has emerged from the midst of that (Island of the Moon), piercing through the great Kula, in the worlds within the sky of the divine firmament, devouring (all things from) within the cavity of the circle of the lower worlds. tanmadhyanirgatamahākulavedhayantīˆ [k gh, g: -yanti] divyāntariknagaganāntarabhūtalenu | pātālacakravivarāntaragrāhayantīˆ [k: -grāha * ntīˆ; gh: grāha * ntī] namāmi paścimakramānvayaśrīkukārām [g: -kujārāˆ; gh: - māmvayaśrīkukākhā] || CMSS 1/2 Salutations to the wealth of touch (sparśalaknmī), the supreme (goddess) who, contemplated by the Wheel of Passion (raticakra), sports (observing) the Vow of perpetual intent on the abode of the crevice in which time and timelessness have been eradicated. (The Vow) is the manifestation of self- attainment (that takes place when) the abode divided by the diversity of oneness and duality has been abandoned. (The Vow) is the manifestation of one's own (innate) vibration (svaghūrma), (that takes place when) the supreme nectar of the juice of each state of being has been drunk. kālākālaviluptakandaragharanityānuraktaˆ [g: -karaghara-] vratam

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-TWO 266 40b. Diagram 12. The Triangle of Letters Brahmā A Ö Ka Tha Ta Sa VinSu Rudra 41. This is the triangle of the Stone made of the Twelve Verses described in chapter three. Cf. 3/31-32 and 7/8 ff. Both the Triangle and the Hexagram are full of the energies of the letters distributed systematically within and around them. They are present in the Six Wheels of the subtle yogic body projected into the corners of the Hexagram that are referred to here as the Six Places. The Triangle represents the Voidness of the Transmental in the End of the Twelve. The Hexagram is the subtle body filled with the same energies differentiated into the Six Wheels. 42. Cf. above 30/199cd-201ab and note.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-THREE 1. The passage from 43/4 to the end is reproduced and glossed in the SamP. There it is called the Yugāvatārasūtra. Here it is called the Caturyugāvatārasūtra. 2. SamP: The Siddha called Sāda has authority in the Krta Age. The goddess of the bliss of the northern (seat) is well established. (The Siddha) came (to her). He came (to her) as (the god) whose accomplished state has no beginning (anādisiddhatva). (Next comes) the teaching (saˆketa) concerning the worship of the (deity’s) attendents (parivāra). At the beginning of a rite, (it is customary for) the Brahmin (to mention the names of one’s family members) beginning from oneself (then that of one’s) father, mother, brother, son, grandson, daughter-in-law, daughter, and grand-daughter, one by one. The same is done in order to know the god’s family. (In this way it is clear that) these Siddhas worship (the goddess) Kubjā. sādanāma siddhaƒ krtayuge adhikārī | tin˜hati uttarānandadevī | samāgataƒ [anāgatā] anādisiddhatvenāgataƒ | parivārārcanasaˆketaƒ | yathāsmadādīnāˆ pitāmātābhrātāputrapautrasnunāputrīpautrīnāˆ [-pautrī-amrtīnāˆ] brāhmaSaƒ [-Sa] pūjādau prthak prthak karoti tadvad devaparivārabodhārthaƒ | kubjopāsakāƒ [kubjāpāsaka] siddhā ete | 3. The four Siddhas who revealed the teachings in the four sacred seats in the four Ages belong to the group of Five Siddhas. The missing Siddha of this group is Ananta (see above 25/41ff.). Sādakhya, the first Siddha, embodies the emissive state (visarga) of the deity. As such, he is responsible for the creation of the four sacred seats. This is discussed in the following chapter. Each of the four Siddhas had four disciples each of whom had many others. In each Age the teachings were also imparted to particular kinds of living beings, as listed in the following table. 16. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-THREE 272 14. OÆÆīśa, TūnSīśa and Ciñcīśa are all names of the founder of the Western Transmission in this Age. This is probably the only place where Sthānu appears along with them. The first two are identified with one another below in 46/42ab. Concerning Ciñcīśa see above 7/62ab and for Vrknanātha, his other name, see above 2/29-30ab. The text says that each one of these descended into a ‘particular division’ of the Western Transmission. Clearly these ‘divisions’ are the sacred seats. Thus, we are told indirectly that the four Siddhas of the sacred seats are all the First Siddha variously named.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-FOUR 1. The first half of this chapter (up to line 44/35ab) deals with a Krama of twenty-eight mantras distributed in six units 4-5-6-6-5-2 corresponding to the Four Seats, Five Goddesses, Six Wheels, Six Yoginīs, Five Jewels and the Couple. The first four verses introduce the explanation of these units by outlining how the Krama arises from the Drop of transcendental Śiva, as his omnipotent will. This divine will is the goddess KuSÆalinī, the energy of the Transmental. Initially, she too is in a pure transcendental state of repose (śānti) and then assumes the sixfold form of the Krama, its states, mantras and other constituents by freely limiting her essentially infinite, undifferentiated nature as pure Sound (nāda). In this way she ‘emerges below’ first as Kula — the Triangle and then as Kaula, the Hexagram into which the Krama is emitted. 2. The four states, Beyond Form and the rest, mentioned here is a common way of analysing the expanse of reality as spheres within which function the sonic and pneumatic energies of the deity, understood to be universal and transcendental consciousness. There is no need to go into an exposition of the many and complex details of the features of these states and their interconnections. We limit ourselves to note here the context in which these lines appear in the KMT (11/7 = KuKh 44/7) and the previous verse from the ±SS (28/22cd-3ab = KuKh 44/5cd- 6ab). The KMT presents these four states as the foundation of the Six Categories (na˜padārtha), which are the well known Six Wheels (na˜cakra). This is achieved in the following passage by the discovery of a sequence of four, then five and finally six conditions of these four states that are related to the Six Wheels: The transmission (krama) of the Divine Command, (divyājñā), that is, the lineages of the currents of the line of teachers (santati), has emerged (jāta) from Śiva who, without beginning or end, is the supreme cause (of all things). (4) [. . .] O Great Mother, know that the primordial Yoni is the supreme one of the supreme (reality). It is the supreme will that, associated with the four, Beyond Form and the others, is of four kinds. Beyond Form is Kāmākhya. Form is the great PūrSagiri. Word is said to be Jālandhara, while the Body is said to be OÆra (= KuKh 44/7). The last (of these) is nectar (then the others are) subtle, very subtle and the first (respectively) making four. The first relationship (these have with ultimate reality) is said to be that with the god Akuleśvara. From Beyond Form comes the Supreme Drop which, radiant, is sustained by Śakti. Then comes Sound, the Blockage (nirodha) and the Half Moon, in due order. This is called the Pentad, the great dawning of the Jewel of Knowledge. She should be known to be the Supreme Yoni, the ocean of the path of action. (4, 6-10)

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-FOUR 281 context it would be more relevant to praise the goddess as the source of the Śrīkrama. 24. ‘Night and day’ are the two streams of the vital breath — prāSa (exhalation) and apāna (inhalation). The syllable that conjoins them and maintains the alternation between them is HA¤SA, the Unstruck Sound of the energy of KuSÆalinī that flows within them. This is the pure consciousness which is the essential nature (citsvarūpa) of all living beings, even the gods 25. ‘Divine drink’ (divyapāna) normally denotes spirituous liquor, which represents the inebriating inner lunar nectar.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-FIVE 1. These Kulas may be the sacred seats. Elsewhere we are told that the six seats constitute the sixfold Kula (61/23 ff.). In this case these appear to be four. If this is correct and the sequence of the seats is the usual one, the series is as follows: Energy > Bhairava > Akula (OÆÆiyāna) > Vikula (Jālandhara) > Puˆkula (PūrSagiri) > Khakula (Kāmarūpa). cf. 42/14cd ff.. 2. See above 38/11-12 and note. 3. By ‘above’ here is probably meant the End of the Twelve. The supreme form of all the Kramas is in the maSÆala there. Although there may be an outer representation of this maSÆala, it is not essential. But even if there is one, it is to this inner maSÆala that the worshipper of the Krama’s attention should be directed. The Kaula adept may well be engaged in ritual action, even so, his primary concern is with the inner world within his subtle body. Devoid of that inner dimension he is not a true Kaula. This is why the Tantra regularly refers to him as a yogi. Although these Tantras prescribe elaborate ritual procedures for Kaulas, the Krama is also frequently described with no reference to any outer forms. We may understand that the drawing of a maSÆala and the projection of the Krama into it is implied, but this is not essential. The Kaula may practice without performing outer rituals but he is wasting his time if when he does so the processes that are the inner counterparts represented by the outer ritual forms are not taking place. He must, at least, clearly represent them within himself in his imagination, visualizing them as described in the scriptures. 4. The Command is the energy of bliss (ānandaśakti) that generates the bliss that empowers even Deity. Devoid of bliss even the Deity would be powerless. 5. The Six Yoginīs are projected into the corners of the hexagram. The seventh Yoginī is YākniSī who is Rudra’s energy, the Yoni in the centre. See below, 63/8. 6. The twenty-seven divisions are also mentioned in 7/7, 45/53, 58/95 and 60/23. See note to 3/52cd-53ab. In this case the mantras of the Krama of Twenty- seven appear to be those relating to 1) the Four sacred seats 2) the Siddhas of the four sacred seats 3) the Five Jewels 4) The Six Yoginīs 5) the group of five 6) the three triads. Thus this Krama of the Youth is configured 4-4-5-6-5-3. 7. The Couple is Navātman and the Goddess. Presumably, the Lord of the Couple is the former and the ‘Vidyā of one syllable’ is the Goddess in the form of the seed-syllable HSKHPHRE¤ or AI¤. 8. This MudrāmaSÆala is SaˆvartāmaSÆala. See above note to 2/14, cf. 3/164d, 51/24a, 60/17b and 68/49d. 9. We have seen that the KumārikākhaSÆa is called Vimalana˜ka and that it is the ‘Pure Division’ — Vimalabheda of the MBT. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-FIVE 287 vimalārtha, which I have translated literally as ‘pure meaning’ may also mean ‘the sense of the Vimala (section of the MBT)’. 10. It appears from the context that the Krama outlined in the previous chapter is that of the Aged (vrddhakrama), which is a sequence of twenty-eight mantras. It is followed in the first part of this chapter by a brief account the Krama of the Youth (kaumārakrama), which is a sequence of twenty-seven mantras. The goddess now announces that she is going to talk about the Krama of the Child (bālakrama). However, suddenly in the next verse she says that she has explained it. Clearly this part of the text has been lost. 11. The Transmission of the Skyfarer is the Divine Current (divyaugha) expounded in chapter 57. It is, essentially the inner flux of the goddess’s energy in the centre of the maSÆala which empowers the emanation through the Kramas within it. In this way they are ‘conjoined’ to it. 12. Cf. above 45/31-32. 13. See chapter 18. 14. See chapter 19. 15. See chapters 9 to 12. 16. Presumably these are the Five Jewels; see chapter 62. 17. See above 45/29. 18. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-SIX 1. We have seen in chapter thirteen that the Kubjikā Tantras accept several variant forms of the Sāˆkhya division of reality into principles of existence (tattva). In the following passage the principles are twenty-five, conveniently distributed in the five sacred seats of the goddess’s Triangle. Here, as elsewhere, the Triangle filled with the principles of existence is called Yogapī˜ha (46/9, cf. above, 38/28-9 and below 46/9 and 46/21). Sometimes we find that the syllable AI¤ is also called Yogapī˜ha (see 38/28-29 and 58/92cd-97ab) and, indeed, the entire SaˆvartāmaSÆala is called that when it is contemplated in the End of the Twelve (see notes to 2/18 and 7/46-47ab). Diagram 13. The Trees of the Sacred Seats P OÆÆiyāSa Jālandhara — Bilva Tree (South) ūrSagiri — Ciñca Tree (North) Tisra (above) Kāmarūpa — Kadamba Tree (in front) 2. pī˜habhūtāni can also be understood to be an attributive compound qualifying an implied mahābhūtāni in which case the meaning would be: ‘(These) are said to be (the elements) as the sacred seats.’ 3. Tisra, the fifth sacred seat, is located above the triangle that contains the other four. The triangle is often identified, amongst other things, with Meru.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-SIX 352 intercourse. She is the red menses of the Yoginī who couples when she is menstruating thereby filling her partner with pure divine Light and bliss. 163. See above note to 46/237-238ab. 164. See 6/90cd-92ab and note. This verse explains the deep, spiritual nature of the three ‘Ms’, namely madya — wine, maithuna — the fluids produced by sexual intercourse and māˆsa — meat. Inebriated with the bliss of the wine he drinks by means of Yoga, the yogi is instructed to consume the two breaths, the inhaled breath and the exhaled breath, which are the gross, outer manifestations of the Sound (nāda) and the Drop (bindu) by conjoining them. This is the meat the yogi eats. Nourished, strengthened and energized by them, he applies himself to attain the supreme state. This is the union of Śiva and Śakti, the individual and the universal and with them all the opposites. This is the supreme form of sex (maithuna) and it is the supreme state the initiate attains by uniting with his partner, a state which is his partner's inherent nature. These are the three Ms in their highest, most authentic form. The KVN (8/95-6) says: Wine (surā) is Śakti. Meat is Śiva and the one who eats it is Bhairava himself. The bliss that arises by the oneness of these two is said to be liberation. Bliss is the nature (rūpa) of Brahman established in the body. Wine is the one that makes it manifest which is why yogis drink it. 165. Presumably this mark (tilaka) is made in between the eyebrows with the sacrificial wine and then contemplated as the Bhairavī of the Drop. 166. The word viknepa literally means ejeculation

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FORTY-SEVEN 1. Concerning the worship of Va˜uka and his mantra, see above 11/33cd- 34ab. Va˜uka (Child) Bhairava is often identified with Skanda-Kumāra who has, like the Va˜uka described here, six heads. In Kaula sources and in his mantras Va˜uka is regularly praised as Skanda normally is, that is, as the son of the goddess (devīputra). Three chapters of the KuKauM are dedicated to the worship of deities on the lunar days. The sacrifice offered on the sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight is dedicated to Kumāra (i.e. Va˜ukabhairava). He is worshipped along with his consort (śakti) in the middle of four attendent Va˜ukas who sit on lotuses in the primary quarters and four maids (dūtī) in the secondary ones. Va˜uka here sits on a peacock, which is Skanda’s vehicle. Va˜uka is said to be in the middle. Now listen to (a description of his) form. Brilliant like heated gold, he has six faces and sixteen arms and is seated on a peacock. He has beautiful hair and speaks pleasantly. He shines with the necklaces and bracelets (he wears). A sacred thread hangs on his shoulder. madhye ca va˜ukaˆ proktaˆ tasya rūpaˆ śrSunvātaƒ | taptacāmīkaraprakhyaˆ naÆvaktraˆ barhisaˆsthitam || dviran˜a ca karā devaˆ sukeśaˆ priyavādinam | hārakeyūrakhacitaˆ skandhe yajñopavītinam || KuKauM 9/129-130 The seven Mothers are born from the god as aspects of the power of his will (icchāśakti). Va˜uka, also called Vīrabhadra, who precedes them and GaSeśa, who follows after them, arose out of them. In the following visualization found in the ŚM Va˜uka, the ‘son of the goddess’, is identified with Vīrabhadra: He has matted hair tied up on top of his head with a snake. The god has a pleasing face and divine, auspicious eyes. A beautiful and divine palmleaf is on his left ear. LambakarSa serves as the ornament for his right ear. He has two arms and holds a vīSā. He has a snake as a sacred thread. The right leg is lifted up and his left thigh is bent. A cloth (covers him) tied to his right knee. O Supreme Goddess, there are gold bracelets on both (his arms) and a snake. Naked and ithyphallic he stands on a great royal throne. One should worship (him), the son of the goddess, as Vīrabhadra by name. ūrdhvajū˜adharaˆ [kh: urddhakū˜a-] divyaˆ coragena [kh: cāragena ca; g: coragrena] nibandhanāt [kh: vaˆdhanāt] | prasannāsyadharaˆ devaˆ [g: devī] divyanetradharaˆ [kh: netra * *] śubham [kh: vikāśitaˆ] ||

english: CHAPTER SIXTY-THREE The Plane of the Hexad of the Command. The venerable (goddess) Vakrā said: Now listen, I will tell (you about) the plane (of realisation) (bhūmikā) of the Hexad of Knowledge (jñānana˜ka). There is the Yoginī (called) Six (±aÆi) of the six principles along with a seventh.1 (1) The Yoginī of the Six Yoginīs The six (collectively) are the seventh Vidyā. The six (naÆi) are the Kula consisting of the group of seven.2 Their authority over knowledge is established from the teaching concerning the Peak (syllables of these Yoginīs).3 (2) It is a single syllable with six letters and belongs to the City of the Moon. Kuleśvarī is born in the Kula of (Hara) the King who is the lunar orb (candrabimba).4 (3) And she has come forth from that body (of the god and entered) into the Cave Dwelling of the Kadamba (Tree). And the six goddesses who are (also) there reside on their natural plane (of being).5 (4) These seven Kula deities are those of the division of the sevenfold Command. Hara is the benefactor on the mountain of Meru, the king of the Kula mountain.6 (5) The deity of the six, which is the Shade of Hara7, has arisen within Hara's bliss and (so) there are six cave-dwelling goddesses of the (Hexagram which is the) original image (bimba)8 of the Abode of the Cave (guhālaya). (6) (When) the activity (that) generates the seed-syllables (sabījakaraSakriyā) (takes place) in accord with the teaching concerning the six sacred seats then (the one) sixfold energy (naÆiśakti) with (its) divisions (operates) in the field of the locations (in the maSÆala) with seed-syllables (sabījasthānagocarā).9 (7)

sanskrit: 232 कुमारिकाखण्ड: विप्राः पूज्यन्ति” सतत श्रीमच्चन्द्रपुरे” गृहे । योन्येका रुद्रशक्तिश्च याक्षिणीनाम देवता ।। ८ ।। नायकी मन्त्रमार्गस्य तया“ क्रममधिष्ठितम्” । अधिकारमशेषस्य सन्तानस्य विशेषतः ॥ ९ ॥ ५३ प्रथमान्वयमेतद्धि” देवताः सप्त मातर: । ५६ ५७ आधारादि तुळे आज्ञान्त गृहस्थानानि षड् विदुः ॥ १० ॥ संस्थिता वाममार्गेण अनामा षडिदेवता “ । ६१ तेऽपि साकारभूताश्च इन्द्रियेषु सचेतसः ।। ११ ॥ प्लवन्ति१२ गगनाम्भोभिमीतर्यो नात्र संशयः । तेषां १४ च सारथी विद्या कर्तरी वामदेवता ॥ १२ ॥ तिष्ठते दक्षिणे द्वारे भगाह्लादेन दक्षिणा । ७२ डरलकसहया देव्यो” मन्त्रस्याक्षरसप्तभिः ॥ १३ ॥ प्रथमान्वयविख्यातं” आदि–आज्ञावतारितम्” । ७६ सप्तमुद्रा गुहास्त्रीणि त्रीणि एकगुहालयम् ॥ १४ ॥ एवं गुहोपदेश तु संवर्ते संप्रवर्तते । एतेषां” मण्डले याग” षट्सु षट्सु प्रकारतः संस्थितं मन्त्रमार्गेण¨ घटस्फोटोपदेशकम् । ८३ ॥ १५ ॥ डकारा चाम्बिकैका च एकाराक्षरत्रिक्रमा ँ ।। १६ ।। एका“ सप्तभिर्भित्त्वा तदा निग्रहमाचरेत् ।
english: CHAPTER SIXTY-THREE 233 Brahmins worship (her) constantly in (the Point) the venerable City of the Moon. (She is) the one Yoni and Rudra's power, the deity called YākniSī.10 (8) She is the leader (nāyakī) of the Path of Mantra.11 She presides over the Transmission (krama) which is the authority (adhikāra) over everything, especially, the lineage (santāna). (9) Indeed, this is the first lineage (anvaya),12 namely, the deities (known as) the Seven Mothers.13 (The wise) know that the locations of the Houses14 beginning with the Foundation up to the (Wheel of the) Command are six. (10) The deity of the six (naÆidevatā),15 (the goddess) Anāmā (the Nameless)16 is established (and made manifest) by (following) the left path.17 They too have arisen, with form (sākāra) and consciousness (sacetasa) in the senses. (11) Verily (they are) the Mothers who exude with the waters of the Void.18 Their Vidyā is that of Charioteer,19 the deity of the left (vāmadevatā) who does (all things) (kartarī). (12) She stands at the southern door20 and is propitious (dakniSā) as the bliss of the Yoni. The goddesses are Õa, Ra, La, Ka, Sa, Ha and Ya along with the seven syllables of the mantra.21 (13) This (group of Seven Mothers) is said to be the first lineage22 that was brought down (to earth) by the first Command. (Here) there are seven Gestures,23 three Caves, (a group of) three and one Cave Dwelling.24 (14) The teaching concerning the caves operates in this way in the Saˆvarta (maSÆala). Their sacrifice takes place within the maSÆala in (each of the groups of) six in accord with (its) parts (prakāra). (15) The Seven Yoginīs Õākinī The teaching concerning the shattering of the jar (of the body) is established by the Path of Mantra.25 One mother is the letter Õa. She is the triple transmission of the letter E. Once one has broken through the letter E with the seven, one should practice restraint (nigraha).26 (16-17ab)

sanskrit: 234 कुमारिकाखण्डः ९३ रकारा तेजसंभिन्ना हरमध्योदरा तथा ॥ १७ ॥ खसंज्ञाज्ञानमात्रा” च षड्भिर्भेदक्रमात्मनि । लकारा चलमध्यस्था लत्रिका पञ्चभेदिता ॥ १८ ॥ १०२ नियोगज्ञानमेकत्र लकारे स्वाधिकारिका' । ककारा च ककारान्ते कद्वये संपुटीकृता ॥ १९ ॥ कमध्यस्था खरूपस्य काकाकारात्मकाकिनी । । शाकिनी शशिमध्यस्था शकारोदरभूषिता ।। २० ।। क्षुद्रकर्मप्रभावेन शकारान्तरशाकिनी' । १०८ हाकिनी हंसमध्यस्था हंसहंसचतुष्टये ।। २१ ।। विग्रह च वियोगस्य हाकिनी व्योममध्यतः ११३ याकिनी जन्ममध्यस्था” कुलषट्कविभेदिता ।। २२ ।। कल्लोलनाडिदमना”“ याकिनी परमेश्वरी । ।
english: CHAPTER SIXTY-THREE 235 Rākinī The (Yoginī of the) letter Ra is conjoined with radiant energy and contains the centre of Hara.27 She is the measure (which is the energy) within the knowledge of the Void (khasaˆjñājñāna) (along) with (the other) six in the essential nature of the sequence of the divisions. (17cd-18ab) Lākinī The (Yoginī of the) letter La, is within the (universal) activity (of the goddess) (cala). (She consists) of three Las conjoined with the five. Her own authority, (she is) the knowledge of application (niyogajñāna) within the letter La. (18cd-19ab) Kākinī The (Yoginī of the) letter Ka is within the letter Ka and is encapsulated between two Kas. Kākinī (the female crow) whose form is that of a crow resides in the middle of the Ka (of the reality) whose form is the Sky. (18cd-20ab) Śākinī Śākinī is in the middle of the Moon and is adorned with the container of the letter Śa. By the power of magic (knudrakarman) Śākinī is within the letter Śa. (20cd-21ab) Hākinī The female Gander, Hākinī, is in the middle of the Gander within the four (syllables): HA¤SA HA¤SA. Hākinī is the form (vigraha) of disjunction in the middle of the Void. (21cd-22ab) Yākinī Yākinī is in the middle of the (place of) birth and is conjoined with the group of six Kulas. Yākinī, who controls the Channel of the Waves (of KuSÆalinī), is the Supreme Goddess (parameśvarī). (22cd-23ab)

sanskrit: 236 कुमारिकाखण्ड: ११९ सप्तसप्तकभेदेन सप्तसप्तपुराज्ञया ॥ २३ ॥ १२० ।। सप्तकूटाः क्रमात् ” सप्त सप्तसप्ताष्टमं पदम् २३ । । अष्टमं च २४ पद१२५ नाम पदमष्टाक्षराणि २६ च ।। २४ ।। वियोगादपि सिद्ध्यन्ते समुद्रादपि सप्तभिः । १२९ १३० सप्तभिश्च स्वरा जाता रुद्रा: सप्तकसप्तभिः सप्तभिश्चौघसंकेत” सप्तसप्तकुलक्रमम् । १३४ सप्तोद्यता'३ समुद्द्योता: ४ सप्तमस्वरसंज्ञया' १३७ हृदयं सप्तदेवीनां हृदयं पञ्चभिर्युतम् । १३९ १३१ ।। २५ ।। १३५ ।। २६ ।। हृदयं सप्तधा भिन्न” सप्तभिन्नकुलस्य च ।। २७ ।। अकुलस्य अभिन्नाख्या मुद्रा कापालिनी भवेत्” । १४२ १४३ सप्तमस्य कपालं तु कपालस्य तु सप्तमम् ।। २८ ।। १४६ सप्तमाज्ञा शिवोऽनन्त: कपाल५ सप्तधा गतम् ' डकारस्य¨ कपालस्य कर्कटीनामदेवता ॥ २९ ॥ विप्रयोगेन बलवान् कपालं डादिभेदितम् १४९ १५२ । । डादिग डादिमध्यस्थ “” उकारत्रयपञ्चभि:' ।। ३० ।। पञ्चाभिज्ञानबोधेन'३ डकार षट्प्रकारतः १५६ १५५ । रकारस्य कपालस्य हाटकी नाम राक्षसी ।। ३१ ।। ·९५७ १५८ । महामेलापके युद्धे रकपाल ५७ रकत्रयम्
english: CHAPTER SIXTY-THREE 237 By the division of the seven groups of seven and by the Command of the abode of seven times seven (seed-syllables) there are, in due order, seven Peak (syllables) and the eighth part (of the mantra) (pada), which is that of the seven times seven (collectively).28 (23cd-24ab) The eighth part (of the mantra) is a part (pada) consisting of eight letters. They are successful even by disjoining (them) from the Ocean (of the core maSÆala) with the seven.29 (24cd-25ab) The vowels are generated by the seven and the Rudras (who govern the letters) by the seven groups of seven. The convention of the current which is the Kulakrama consisting of the seven times seven is due to the seven. (25cd-26ab) They have arisen from the seven and shine radiantly along with the one called the seventh vowel (r). (It is) the heart of the seven goddesses, the Heart endowed with the five (PraSavas). The Heart of the Kula that is divided into seven is divided into seven. (26cd-27) The Seven Yoginīs of the Skulls30 Karka˜ī — Õākinī The Gesture of Kapālinī31 of Akula is said to be undivided (abhinna). The Skull (is the goddess) of the seventh (syllable) and the seventh (syllable is that) of the Skull. (28) The seventh (aspect of the) Command is Śiva who has no end.32 Karka˜ī is the deity of the Skull which is the letter Õa. (29) The powerful Skull is by (this initial) differentiation (viprayoga) (of the letters) conjoined with (the letters) beginning with Õa. Present in (the letters) beginning with Õa it is within (the series) begining with Õa along with the five and the three of the letter Ū. By awakening the five signs (abhijñāna), the letter Õa becomes sixfold.33 (30-31ab) Hā˜akī — Rākinī Hā˜akī is the female demon (rāknasī) of the Skull which is the letter Ra. The Skull Ra in the Battle of the Great Union and three RAKAs.34 (31cd-32ab)
