english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FIFTY-EIGHT 1. This chapter is the same as chapter twenty-eight of YKh (1). We come across three versions of the Root Sūtra above in chapters 26, 38 and 42. See also chapter twenty-six of the AS which also deals with the Command of the Plane and is related to the Root Sūtra. 2. Concerning the double meaning of the word 'bhūmikā' as both 'explanation' and 'plane of being or realisation', see note to 59/4. 3. YKh (1) reads instead: ‘the group of six sacred seats’ (pī˜hana˜ka). This variant reading suggests that the main group of six is the group of six sacred seats. This makes sense. The six seats are located in the corners of the hexagram that surrounds the triangle that constitutes the core of the goddess's maSÆala. A hexagram consists of two triangles — one facing down and the other facing up — superimposed on one another. The downward facing triangle is the Yoni and the upward facing one is the Li‰ga. Thus the two represent the union of the goddess and the god, the Yoni and the Li‰ga which is, as the text tells us, sixfold and contains the six sacred seats. From this union all things are generated and so is said to be the universal cause of all things. The essential nature of the conjunctio is the bliss experienced within it, that is, within the feminine. This is the inner potential state that contains and is the source of the hexagram which represents the outer manifest form of the conjunctio. The inner conjunction takes place within the Yoni which is the Triangle with the syllable AI¤ in the centre. The hexagram that surrounds it represents the consciousness of the bliss experienced in the Yoni when union takes place. This chapter describes this inner state — bhūmikā — of the Root, that is, the syllable AI¤ and the ‘sūtra’, the surrounding Triangle that together make up the most essential part of the maSÆala (58/12cd-13).

The black colour symbolizes the unmanifest, that is, the 'unillumined' condition of the transcendental Void. This is the domain of the dark aspect of the goddess where she is Kālikā (the Little Black Virgin), the New ('Black') Moon hidden within Bhairava, whose body is the black, moonless sky. This is the primordial, original sacred seat of the deity, the Triangle of the hidden moon in the centre of which is the Yoni that contains all the archetypal energies of the letters, seed-syllables and mantras. This state is represented by the syllable AIM to which are added the Five Praṇavas. Together these six are the Linga of Space (ākāśalinga) whose six aspects, each a Linga of Space in its own right, are described below (58/43cd-54). See notes to 58/70cd-72ab, 83cd-84ab, 60/3, 31-32ab. , This chapter presents a series of verbal images of the Triangle and the syllable AIM. The presentation is intentionally cryptic in order to keep the teaching secret. This is achieved by naming what are essentially the same 'things' in many ways. The Five Praṇavas are probably arranged around Vägbhava in the manner they are arranged around the fire pit when they are represented by their icons. Four are in the primary directions and the fifth, Sadāśiva, in the middle. See

The account returns repeatedly to this basic configuration, examining its parts and the relationship they have with one another. 6. Diagram 4. The Bhagīśa Li‰ga (1) 7. The transcendental Darkness represented by the Triangle is the divine body of the Goddess. It is the Sky, that is, the Void from which the Li‰ga in which she resides emerges. Normally, the goddess emerges from the god. In this case, it seems that this basic model is reversed, but this is not really so. The transcendental Yoni generates another Yoni. This is the immanent ‘male’ Yoni, the Li‰ga Bhagīśa. Also called the Wheel of Meru, it is the Point within the Triangle that encompasses it. 8. In order to understand this and what follows, it is necessary to remember the basic principle that the container is the contained and that they emerge from one another even as they merge back into each other in the dynamism of the Emptiness from which the universe of words and their objects emanates. Thus here we are told that the original Void, the Great Cave, is ‘contained’ in the Li‰ga emitted from it. The Great Cave is the Point above the Half Moon. It represents the essentially transcendental emptiness of Bhagīśa Li‰ga, the Point. This is the place of the Moon in the Cave. The Moon in the Cave is the Point, the Lord of the Cave. Thus the container — the Void — and its content — the Point — are one. The Point (Bindu) is the Full Moon and the Half Moon (Ardhacandra) is the New Moon. The Full Moon drips its nectarine energies into the New Moon even as the Full Moon emerges out of the New Moon. Thus the two nourish one another. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FIFTY-NINE 1. Chapters 59 to 64 of the KuKh are taken wholesale from chapter 29 to 31 of YKh (1). They are an exposition of the Krama of YKh (1) which is the Kaumārakrama of Twenty-seven parts (KuKh 59/1-2ab) in six groups of mantras divided 4-5-6-4-5-3. These correspond to the four sacred seats (KuKh chapters 59 to 61), the Five Jewels (Ratnapañcaka) (KuKh chapter 62), the Six Yoginīs (Jñānana˜ka) (KuKh chapter 63), the Pure Pentad (Vimalapañcaka) and the Triad (Trikabheda) (KuKh chapter 64). These chapters present complex, and often obscure, ‘esoteric explanations’ (bhūmikā) of the energies of the planes of existence (bhūmikā) to which they correspond. Most of chapter 66 is YKh (1) 33 that deals with the Octad of Kula associated with this Krama. The end of YKh (1) 33, which is the conclusion of this long section, is KuKh 65/1-22. 2. YKh (1) (29/10cd) adds: That is accomplished by its esoteric meaning (bhūmikārtha). Tell me (that so that people) may attain liberation. bhūmikārthena saˆsiddhaˆ kaivalyārthaˆ vadasva me || 3. The teaching of Kulakaula is the maSÆala. Here this is understood to be its basic essential core — the Triangle of which the sonic counterpart is the syllable AI¤. Kula is the triangular body of the syllable AI¤. This Triangle is the letter E which in the following verse is called the ‘pure form’ of AI¤. It is the core of it without the additions that convert it from E to AI¤. The three syllables HRĪ¤ ŚRĪ¤ KLĪ¤ are on the corners of the Triangle (see intro. 1, p. 273). Thus it is called Trikū˜a — the mountain with three peaks or, occasionally, the ‘letter Ī tripled’ (58/63cd-64ab and 59/5). Kaula, which is derived from Kula, comprises the permutations of Kula. Internally they are the upper additions to the Triangle. Externally, Kaula is the Hexagram (39/24). 4. The term bhūmikārtha is difficult to translate because it has two meanings that relate to aspects of the teaching and the reality that is taught. From the first point of view the bhūmikārtha is the explanation of the Root Sūtra which describes in its own symbolic language the parts of the maSÆala and its sonic contents and counterparts. In this sense ‘bhūmikā’ means simply ‘explanation’. The term ‘bhūmikā’ also denotes the energy of the ‘bhūmi’, that is, the ‘ground’ of existence represented by the maSÆala and its sonic counterparts. This energy is in a state of perpetual development or ‘expansion’ (vikasvarā) through the phases of manifestation. Understood to be both ‘form’ (rūpa) and ‘sound’ (nāda), the phases of its development are represented in these two parallel aspects, that is, as the parts of the maSÆala that emerge as it being drawn and the energies or phases of sound as the corresponding mantras or syllables are uttered. Both aspects symbolize the experience of the phases of the dynamism of the one reality. This experience, ranging from transcendental Emptiness to that of concrete phenomena, is that of Deity. It is also the experience Deity has of its own nature

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER FIFTY-NINE 154 The eight Kulas are those of the eight Mothers who surround the Hexagram. They govern the energies of the eight categories of letters and so reproduce the energies contained within the central Triangle. Thus they contain the ‘knowledge of Kula’ — ‘the beautiful ocean’ of the Yoni full of the energies of the letters that embody the aspects of the pure consciousness of Bhairava, who the transcendental Void beyond Speech and its energies abides in the midst of them. The energies are aspects of the ‘joy of bliss’ through which Bhairava is realised to be the silent transcendental, liberated Self. 82. Each phase, plane, state, aspect, energy and groups of them, in short every part of the maSÆala is a plane of realisation, which when fully experienced is realised to be the whole reality, the fully liberated state. This is achieved by the grace of the deity who imparts the Command of Realisation that bestows empowerment and authority (adhikāra) (see intro. vol. 1, p. 210 ff.).

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY 1. This chapter is drawn from YKh (1) (30/1-99 = KuKh 60/1-92) and YKh (2) (32/32-57 = KuKh 60/75-100). 2. This and the following chapter reply to this question. It appears at first sight that very little is said about the Siddhas. But this is not so. The main concern is with the inner representations of the six sacred seats and the Wheels, energies, Sound and the other inner realities related to them. These are important because they house the beings who govern the forces and processes they contain. These are the Siddhas and the Goddesses. As we travers one center to the next we encounter the Siddhas and their energies one by one and so pass from one aspect to the other of the inner experience of the Krama. These are sacred seats of the lineage (anvaya) (61/46). This then is the awareness (vicāra) of the Siddhakrama (61/37cd-38), the Current of the Siddhas that flows through the phases of emanation that correspond to the stages and aspects of this contemplation. 3. The instruments (YKh (1) reads ‘causes’) of realisation are the energies configured in the centers within the body of the deity. These are the ‘rays’. Internally, they are the building blocks of the experience deity has within itself in which the Yogi participates as he comes to know and experience them. Externally, they operate analogously in the construction of outer experience. They are represented by the Five PraSavas. Collectively these ‘rays of knowledge’ are the Great Knowledge of pure consciousness. The Tortoise in the Navel is the Point in the centre of the Triangle. All outer forms and energies merge into the Void in the Centre and the world order with all its levels, worlds and principles fuse into a single Principle and are withdrawn into the Void like the tortoise withdraws its limbs into its shell. Knowledge of how this is done, by means of profound contemplation, is the Great Knowledge. According to another possible translation: ‘It is the consciousness (vijñāna) of the Supreme Lord (experienced) when the energies of the Tortoise in the Navel have been consumed.’ 4. Pārameśvara is both one of the names of the MBT (see, for example, above 39/80ab) and the Kubjikā school as a whole (see, for example, above 30/73cd, 117ab and 39/150). I suppose the latter sense is meant here. See above note to 46/263-264 and cf. the expression vijñānaˆ pārameśvaram below in 64/97ab. 5. Concerning the tortoise seat, see 48/20-21ab, 55/7 and, especially, the note to 57/87cd-88.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-ONE 1. This chapter continues with the exposition of the remaining groups of six that constitute the unfolding experience of the planes of realisation of this part of the Krama. The previous chapter dealt with the sacred seats, the following passage opens with a presentation of the goddesses and Siddhas who reside in the sacred seats from the same sophisticated metaphysical perspective. 2. There is essentially only one sacred seat in the body (60/83), one Li‰ga (61/20cd), one Kula, one Siddha (61/39) and only one bliss (60/49cd-50). Each is the one reality variously understood and each is sixfold. In the same way there is only one goddess who, in consonance with the six planes of realisation marked by the seats, progressively unfolds along with them revealing herself as the goddess within each one of them. Moreover, in accord with the common principle of the logic of this symbolic system, each goddess is the one goddess who is all of them (see for example, 61/8 and 61/10). 3. YKh (2) (34/2cd) reads this sentance: And she is the leader of the sacred seats who with the six (seats) illumines relative distinctions. pī˜hānāˆ [k, kh: pī˜hanāˆ] nāyikā [k, kh: nāyakāˆ] caiva naÆbhirbhedaprakāśinī [k, kh: -prakāśinām] || Bhairava is the Self who illumines and the goddess gives him Light. 4. YKh (2) 34/3cd: She is progressively established and dissolves away in the course of churning (manthāna) the six sacred seats (manthāne kramaśaƒ [k, kh: kramadho] sthitā ||). 5. Cf. 59/4. 6. According to presentation of the five seats above in chapter six Khageśī is the goddess of this seat who is said to be ‘well known as Kubjikā’ (6/31, cf. 61/23). Kubjikā is the Moon (7/55cd-56ab) who emanates from the core of Śiva’s being as the light of the moon (7/52cd-53ab and note). Kubjikā is Khageśvarī because she moves in the Sky of Pure Consciousness. She is Nityaklinnā (the Perpetually Wet One) (59/68cd-69ab) because she oozes with the juice of consciousness secreted from the Point in the centre of her Yoni. In this representation of the six sacred seats Kubjikā in these two aspects is present in all of them as Śavarī (also called Samarī, see note on 6/65) identified with the Yoginī Ko‰kaSā who is the deity of all the seats (61/10). The Śavarī of each seat generally has two names. Each of them develops an aspect of the experience of the highest reaches of expanded consciousness. Here these six are said to be aspects of the letter E. Elsewhere, however, they are said to be aspects of the letter A, which is the phonemic representation of the goddess Anāmā (61/22). english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-TWO 1. The remaing five parts (prakāra) of the Krama are presented in this and the following two chapters. The Five Jewels is the subject of this chapter and the Hexad of the Knowledge, the following one. The remaining three groups are presented in chapter sixty-four. The Five Jewels invoke the millions of Yoginīs who reside in five worlds of the sky (gagana), heaven (svarga), wind (pavana), mortals (martya), and hell (nāraka). Their mantras — ‘jewels of nectar’ — are referred to by the initials of these five worlds simply as Ga Sa Pa Ma Na. The Jewels invoke the protection of the billions of Yoginīs of the five worlds. The KMT (18/59-64) says of this group of mantras that: Vāgeśvarī (A), Māyā (I), and Mohanī (U), the third, Jñānadevī (E) and Gāyatrī (O), these are said to be the Five Jewels. Possession (by the goddess) (āveśa) takes place by just depositing (this group on the body) and by its enounciation it takes place clearly. This (possession) binds together (bandhana) the body (piSÆa) and destroys evil mantras (siˆha) [ . . . ] The goddess has as her limbs the Jewels and her body is made of them. Listen to the teaching concerning the Jewels. The Jewels are said to be nectar. O beloved, the nectar is of five kinds. The body (piSÆa) is bound together by that (group of five mantras) without that there is no life. [ . . . ] There is the Jewel of the nectar of the sky (gagana), the Jewel of the nectar of heaven (svarga), the Jewel of the nectar of the (world of the) wind, that of mortals (martya) and hell (nāraka). (This is the) group of Five Jewels. It is born from the goddess's body and has come out from it. Endowed with vitality (savīrya), it is the vitality of knowledge (jñānavīrya). (But) if (this group of mantras) is unknown, it destroys (the body’s) vitality. The Five Jewels are related to the five Kaula sacrificial offerings (pañcopacāra) of feces (viśvaknāra), urine (mūtra), blood (rakta), fat (vasā) and semen (śukra). Governed by the gods of the Five PraSavas, these are the Five Potions of Immortality (amarīdravya) (see note to 29/43 for reference from µīkā MS K fl. 65a). Another group of five bodily substances are the ‘substances of the Rule’ (samayadravya): 1) blood 2) meat 3) bone 4) marrow taken from a skull and 5) skin. Properly propitiated, the Jewels vitalize these substances in the body. Otherwise, they depleat them in one’s own body and can be induced to do so in the body of others. As the KMT (18/70cd-73) says: When they are known they illumine with their energizing radiance (dīpti). When unknown, they take away (that) radiance. The power of the Jewels is unparalleled and they burn with brilliant flames. O fair lady, by their power the

The Five Jewels are a part of the Krama, which is the root of this group of mantras, as it is of the others that constitute the Krama. The Krama is thus the ‘teacher’ of these five mantras just as it is of the others it contains. Above (60/38cd-39ab) we find the expression ‘pī˜hakramācāra’ — ‘the practice of the Krama of the sacred seats’. In this case ‘krama’ also means ‘sequence’. Thus the expression means essentially the worship of the sacred seats successively one after another. There the seats are the six projected into the Hexagram. Each seat corresponds to one of the six parts (prakāra) of the Krama that are also projected into the Hexagram, serving there as their ‘containers’ and sources. 106. The ‘five groups of five’ are outlined above in 62/50-52. 107. The two emissions are the Sound (nāda) and the Point (bindu) (63/98) of the two breaths. It is hard indeed to experience the liberating and creative flux of energies of the KadambamaSÆala in the centre between them. YKh (1) inserts the following line (30/102ab): Having first known (Vāgbhava) this one instrument (of mantra) then (one can understand) the teaching concerning the letters. karaSaikaˆ [k, gh, ‰: karanedaˆ; g: karaSekaˆ] purā jñātvā tadā varSopadeśakam | Power is the Transmental energy of the Command that pervades and empowers the sonic energies contained in the Ocean of the Yoni of the Triangle of Vāgbhava, the ‘instrument’ of mantra and the body of the goddess. 108. Instead of ‘silent’ (tūnSī) here YKh (1) reads ‘fire’ (vahni). See above 62/66.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-THREE 1. The Hexad of Knowledge — Jñānana˜ka, here also called the Hexad of the Command — Ājñāna˜ka, is also called the Hexad of Chastisement — Nigrahana˜ka or Grace — Nugrahana˜ka, depending on its application. The six Vidyās are those of the six Yoginīs — Õākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī and Hākinī. They are commonly referred to by the first letter of their name as the Hexad beginning with Õā — Õādina˜ka. They are worshipped in the Hexagram with a seventh Yoginī in the centre. She is the supreme goddess (63/23cd-4ab) who is all the six Yoginīs together and so, in a sense, is not a separate one (cf. 63/2, 63). Even so, the Tantra acknowledges her separate identity with the words: ‘the six are the Kula consisting of the group of seven’ (63/2). Accordingly, she is called the ‘Six’ — ±aÆi or the ‘energy of the six’ — ±aÆiśakti. In most accounts, these Yoginīs are linked closely to the vital constituents of the body (dhātu), namely, chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and sperm, respectively (intro vol. 2, p. 29). They live within them in the body and draw their power and vitality from them. Acordingly, they are propitiated by offering these things to them in sacrifice. Satisfied, they protect and maintain the body healthy. Otherwise, angered and hungry they consume the vital essences of those who ignore them. Invoked in black rites (na˜karma) they consume them in the body of the enemy who has been behaved unjustly and especially one who has harmed their cult or its votaries. Worshipped in that context they are called the Fierce Group of Six (ugrana˜ka) or Hexad of Chastisement (nigrahana˜ka). Although the ‘ferocity’ of their power is acknowledged and are called here by the latter name (see note to 63/101), in this presentation the Yoginīs are the deities of the forces, states, energies and mantras of the maSÆala that represents the configurations of the dynamism of consciousness in relation to Deity, the body and the world. The Yoginīs are described from this perspective, one by one, as many as four times in this chapter (63/16-23ab, 28-43ab, 62-75, and 78cd-89). 2. This line also means: ‘±aÆi is the seventh Vidyā. ±aÆi is the Kula consisting of the group of seven’. 3. The Six Yoginīs and their corresponding Vidyās and seed-syllables are projected into the six corners of the Hexagram. In the centre is the seventh. In accord with the basic principle that the container is the contained, she is the embodiment of the six who surround her. The six seed-syllables are formed simply by adding YŪ¤ to the first letter of the Yoginīs' names. Thus they are: ÕYŪ¤, RYŪ¤, LYŪ¤, KYŪ¤, ŚYŪ¤ and HYŪ¤. The Vidyā of the Yoginī in the centre is these six recited together. Thus in the following verse it is said to be ‘a single syllable with six letters’. The Vidyā is Kuleśvarī, the mistress of her Kula and is in the Point in the centre called the City of the Moon. 4. Bhairava, the Self, is the king of the mountain of Kula (61/9 and note,

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-FOUR 1. The first part of this chapter deals with a group of mantras variously called the Five Pure Ones —Vimalapañcaka, the Pentad of the Pure Knowledge — Vimalajñānapañcaka and the Pentad of the Group of Yoginīs - YoginīgaSapañcaka. Like the Group of Six Yoginīs and the Five Jewels, it is a common component of the Kramas. All the parts of the Krama relate to the mind, senses and body (see 2/8-9ab). These five, like the previous two groups, are related to the five senses (64/14, see vol. 3, appendix 9, table 31). The components of the Krama are of three kinds, namely, sacred seats, Siddhas and, as is this group, Yoginīs. However, Campakā is the only Yoginī amongst the five mentioned in this presentation (64/44) although this group of Yoginīs is so important that Kubjinī is amongst them. See version in the ŚM (KuKh vol. 6, appendix 9, table, 22) and explanation and version in the ±SS (ibid. table 31). 2. ‘Repose’ is the condition of the Point in the centre (see note to 64/15) Like the members of the other groups, each of the five members of this one is all the five and all of them are aspects of an original one which is the Supreme Soul in the Point in the centre (64/5). In this case it is the Pure One, just as the one amongst the Five Jewels is called the Great Jewel and the one amongst the Six Yoginīs, the Six. 3. YKh (1) (MSs K, Gh and ¥): The bliss of the repose of the Pure Ones is the (experience of) merger (that takes place) in the (five) instruments (of mantra) that have been (progressively) traversed (ākrānta). Although the pentads are presented here very concisely, groups of five are very powerful. As we read below: wherever power resides, it is fivefold (64/52). The Tantra reiterates repeatedly that the maSÆala, the Point, and the Triangle are fivefold, as is the energy of the Pure One. The mantras and the letters are in groups of five, as are the states that they represent, but these are mostly indicated by no more than strings of names and code words. They alternate between references to mantras, letters and seed-syllables and states and energies to which they correspond in some way. In order to understand these references it is essential to know the mantras, and even that may not be sufficient to make everything clearly intelligible. Possibly further research will reveal a key to unlock the meaning of this particularly cryptic text. In the meantime, I must ask the reader to be patient and rest content with what meaning can be grasped. 4. Here the text explains why they are called ‘pure’. They possess a pure, spiritual power. Morever, they are also purifying. Their presence in the Krama worshipped in the maSÆala purifies it. 5. The Tree has five branches and it grows in the ‘garden’ of the sacred seat of the Point in the centre (64/37).

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-FOUR 278 bhairavāknaramā˜¬Sāˆ [k, gh: -mādyāSāˆ; g: -mātrSāˆ; ‰: bhairavāknaramā * Sāˆ] taddhyānāmitatejasām | 58. The energy of the goddess courses through the letters that ‘rotate’ as it were through her. Absorbed in pure contemplation the Mothers of the letters collect the goddess’s energy. Thus the goddess as KuSÆalinī manifests her power in the Triangle of the energies of the letters governed by Bhairava and his aspects, the Heroes who govern the letters, all of whom, no less than he, are Śiva. She is the triple energy — Mudrā — and the triad of the qualities of Nature — guSa. She resides in the centre of the Ocean of the Triangle as the Point, which is her sonic iconic form as Vāgbhava, the syllable AI¤. This syllable is uttered before each of the letters that have been converted into seed-syllables by the addition of ardhacandra and anusvāra, that is, Sound (nāda) and the Point (bindu). Repeated one after the other from beginning to end, the the Mothers of the letter of the left, that is, Vāgbhava rotate through it even as it shines in the centre between each one absorbed in the final nasalization of each syllable. A third of the way through each cycle the adept utters one of the three syllables he has drawn in the corners of the Triangle accompanied by an empowering Gesture. Just as each letter is infused in this way with the unlimited energy of the goddess similarly, all the letters also receive it collectively by virtue of the goddess’s triadic form as these three. 59. Manmatha, that is, Kāmadeva, is the Point in the centre that is split up and rubbed by the inner churning that generates bliss (58/70cd-72ab). YKh (1) (32/97ab) reads this sentance: The Yogi is always Kāmadeva in the midst of passion (kāma) and the three categories. kāmadevaƒ sadā yogī kāmamadhye [k, gh, ‰: -madhya; ‰: kā * -] trivargagaƒ [k, gh, ‰: trivarSayoƒ; g: -yoƒ] | 60. These are the energies and states within the Point, the Li‰ga which is the formless aspect of the deity. 61. The five listed previously belong to the formless aspect of deity. The six energies are the potencies that manifest as the Hexagram latent in the Point. When the Point is ‘churned’ by the intent which is the intense contemplation of the deity, the Void of the Point assumes the triadic form of the Triangle of the Transmental and the consciousness of the Supreme Lord. He experiences it as the subtle contemplation which is the conception of his intent to make his energies manifest. In this way the universe of phonemic energies ‘matures’ and is formed within the expanse of Deity’s divine consciousness who contemplates its inception within it as the energy contained within the letter A. 62. YKh (1) (32/100cd): The supreme mantra is based on (the letter) A (āśrita). It is the supreme state (gati) beyond mantra. āśritaˆ paramaˆ mantraˆ [k, gh, ‰: maˆtra] mantrātītā parā [g: parā‰] gatiƒ ||

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-FIVE 1. KuKh 65/1-22 = YKh (1) 33/100-122ab. Chapter 66 of our text is most of Chapter 33 YKh (1). The last 22 verses of chapter 33 of YKh (1) appear here in the beginning of chapter 65 of the KuKh. 2. This verse is a variant of 64/99. A ‘hermitage’ is the location of a sacred reality. In this case it is the Triangle that contains Kailāsa. The ‘bliss of sport’ is perfect rest within the Void of the consciousness of deity (64/14). 4. Above (64/53), this treasure chest of knowledge (jñānamañjūna) is called the treasure chest of mantra (mantramañjūnaka). After the six explanatory sūtras — ‘bhūmikās’ — each dealing with one of the six components of the Sequence of Twenty-seven of the Transmission of the Youth (kaumārakrama), chapter 33 of YKh (1) comes as a conclusion. The last verses of that chapter, which are the first 22 verses of this chapter of the KuKh, explain the importance of the bhūmikās (‘explanations’) and so aptly concludes the entire section with its six bhūmikās that extends from chapter 29 to 33 of YKh (1) reproduced in chapters 59 to 66 of the KuKh. Thus the colophon at the end of Chapter 33 of YKh (1) reads: ‘the description concerning the planes (of existence) in the Krama of twenty-seven divisions is complete (saptāviˆśabhedakrame bhūmikādhikāravarSanaˆ samāptaˆ).’ 3. According to 45/35 above, liberation is attained in seven lifetimes. The goddess is reborn in her eighth rebirth (3/160-161). See intro. vol. 1, p. 127. 5. A jar is installed in the middle of the maSÆala within which the main deities and the Krama are worshipped. Thus it represents the Point in the centre which is called the Supreme Jar (see note to 62/42). 6. It is essential not only to know the sequence of emanation but also the location of the entities that have been emanated represented by their mantras or in other ways in the maSÆala. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-SIX 1. KuKh 66/1-90ab has been drawn from YKh (1) 33/1-99. 2. The two polarities are, presumably, Śiva and Śakti. The polarity (pakna) Śiva is mentioned above in 3/133 as the polarity within the Void (vyoman) in which the Vidyā (= Śakti) abides ‘mounted on the Wheel of the Fourth state’ which is the Yoni. Pure transcendence is beyond all polarities, including that of Śiva and Śakti. The first stage in the process of emanation or, to put it another way, the highest level of immanence, is characterized by the formation of this fundamental polarity and, as a consequence, all others. In this verse they are understood as the maSÆala or ‘Wheel’, which is the deployment of the energies that are aspects of Śakti and Śiva who is the possessor of these energies and hence is the ‘Lord of the Wheel’. 3. The triple polarity is represented by the sides of the Triangle. The Point in the centre where Bhairava governs the Wheel is the point of contact, the ‘door’ between immanence and transcendence. There, at the threshold between them, Bhairava on the one side governs the immanent domain, represented by the ‘triple polarity’ and on the other is established in transcendental domain beyond it. On the one side are the ‘three lights’ of Sun, Moon and Fire and on the other the Light of the Self beyond them that illuminates and governs them. 4. It is surprising that Bhairava is identified here with Vāgbhava, which is the syllable of the goddess. Perhaps the text is corrupt, but this is not likely as the reading here is confirmed by YKh (1). Presumably the meaning is that as he is one with the goddess he is also one with her syllable. He is the ‘substance’ as it were of Vāgbhava and she is his energy. Altematively, one could emend to Vāgbhavaripumardakaƒ — 'the slayer of the foes of Vāgbhava'. 5. See note to 65/2. 6. YKh (1): ‘made of the energy of consciousness (cidkalāmaya)’. 7. Cf. 63/78ab, see note to 63/100. 8. The Wheel of the Directions appears to be the Triangle in which the vital breath moves (see 59/55 and note to 59/92). 9. The three Wheels are actually one Wheel and that is essentially Emptiness. It is the Wheel itself, the Void in which it is established and the Void that is within it. 10. YKh (1) reads ambaraˆ for asvaraˆ. While that reading appears at first sight to be the best, this one is supported by a reference below that says that this Wheel is called the ‘Sound of Śiva’, that is, Unstruck Sound (66/38). 11. YKh (1) (33/23cd) reads this sentance: Then the illuminator of the light of the Shade illumines it. tadāsau dyotayecchāyāˆ chāyājyotiprakāśakaƒ |

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-SEVEN 1. Kula is the Triangle, while the Root of Akula is the Point within it, full of the energy of the goddess whose sonic icon is Vāgbhava. The maSÆala that surrounds it is formed from the mantras and goddesses, here called Mudrās, that expand out from the centre where they abide in the form of energies and planes of consciousness. Now that that has been explained in the previous chapters, this one outlines how the twenty-seven principles (tattva) that correspond to the twenty- seven mantras of the Krama exist in the Yogapī˜ha. 2. Generally the word ‘Yogapī˜ha’ denotes the maSÆala on which the scriptures are placed and venerated. By extension the Kubjikā Tantras call the maSÆala in the End of the Twelve Yogapī˜ha (see intro. vol. 1, p. 377). In this case it denotes the Point in the centre of the Triangle which is the ‘empowered (śākta) Li‰ga’ and the ‘essential nature of all the principles’. They all exist there within Bhairava who is the Void which is the ‘great abode of all the worlds’. Held together in the energy of the Void they work together to form her body (piSÆa), the ‘ball’ (piSÆa) of the Point (67/40cd-41ab, 41cd-42ab and 44cd-45ab) here called Yogapī˜ha (the ‘seat of union’) within the three Kramas on the corners of the surrounding Triangle. 3. Reversing the usual serial order of the sequence of emanation, in this case it begins with the Earth principle which is accordingly called the seat of emanation (srn˜ipī˜ha). This is associated with Kāmarūpa, the seat whose ‘form is desire’, as ‘desire’ is emanation. 4. The twenty-five Principles listed in the table are, as one would expect, basically divided into five groups of five. Only the last two are groups of six and four. Apart from four anomalies, which are probably errors, they correspond to sacred seats, goddesses and gods of the seats, Wheels of the subtle body and Yoginīs. 11. english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-EIGHT 1. This chapter begins with a passage (68/1-24ab) describing the visualized form of the goddess. It is drawn from the YKh (1) where it appears as one of a series of four sūtras each dedicated to a description of a form the goddess, three for the three lineages and one undifferented (ninkalā) form beyond. The form described here is that of the goddess of the middle lineage. See intro. vol. 2, p. 174 ff.. 2. These are the colours of the goddess when she appears out of the Li‰ga. See above 5/30 and notes. 3. The goddess’s face is the Yoni because her sonic iconic form is the triangular syllable AI¤. Her form is the Yoni because she is the Triangle of the energies of the Transmental that emanates from the Point in the centre that contains her ‘face’. She possesses six Yonis because she is also the Hexagram that surrounds it. 4. See note to KuKh 3/45. 5. The Thirty-two syllable Samayā Vidyā is that of the goddess as the New Moon. Below in 68/18 she is also said to consist of forty-two syllables. This is the goddess as the Full Moon. The KuKh says that she 'has been encapsulated within the Yoni' (bhagodarapu˜īkrtā). The version in YKh (1) (19/37cd) adds that she is ‘the goddess Full Moon who is completely full and has been encapsulated by both the five' (saˆpūrSā pūSimā devī ubhaupañcapu˜īkrtā). The Vidyā is not just 'encapsulated' by the Yoni but also by the Five PraSavas at the beginning of it uttered in the forward order and five at the end of it uttered in the reverse order, while the Vidyā itself is uttered in reverse (see above 9/58cd-59). This is the form of the Vidyā in the centre of the Triangle (see above, 7/35-6ab and 7/47-9ab). In more essential terms YKh (2) says of the goddess in the Yoni: (The wise) know you (O goddess) to be the Kaulika (reality) there in the oneness of the arising and falling away (of all things). It releases a current of nectar and energizes (Vāgbhava, the goddess’s) PraSava. (She is the goddess of) the Cave of the Yoni (bhagaguhyā) who contains the Yoni present at the beginning of it and in the middle. Arising from the middle and the end of the Yoni she is Amā (the New Moon), the seventeenth energy (of the Moon). Fashioned from sixteen parts, she resides at the End of the Sixteen. udayāstamanaikatve [k: udastamanakatve; kh: -manakatvaˆ] tatra tvaˆ kaulikaˆ viduƒ [k, kh: vidu] || muñcate amrtaughaˆ [k, kh: amrtoghaˆ] ca dīpanaˆ praSavasya ca | bhagādyā bhagamadhyasthā bhagaguhyā bhagodarī || bhagamadhyāntajātā [k: -madhānta-; kh: kh: -madhāntajāto] ca amā saptadaśī

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-EIGHT 340 First Sacred Seat. The first of all repostories of the scripture and its teachings. The colophons constantly remind us that it is from here that the ‘primordial descent into the great sacrifice of the Churning Bhairava’ has taken place. The great mantra of the original scripture is ‘extracted’ directly from there. 62. The YKh (1) presents a hierarchy of six systems (darśana) which are then followed by four Kaula āmnāyas, not mentioned in the KuKh. These are discussed in intro. vol. 2, p. 340 ff.. 63. Cf. above 68/111. 64. The first group of the scriptures in this ascending hierarchy is a series of seven traditions, namely, Buddhist, Jaina, Vedic, Saura, Sāˆkhya, VainSava, and Yogaśāstra. Then come the scriptures of the Pāśupatas, of which four kinds are listed, namely, Mahāvrata, Vimala, Lākula and Pāśupata. Above them are the Śaiva scriptures of ‘many kinds’. These are probably the Siddhānta Āgamas. Above are the Bhairava Tantras. As Bhairava is the ninth Void beyond Samanā (78-80), we have reached the Tantras that belong to the sphere of Mind Beyond Mind and the Transmental. Above we are told that there are eight Bhairava Tantras (68/130), but only six are mentioned, although the number eight is reached by the addition of three homonyms of Svacchanda Bhairava (i.e. Bahurūpa, Aghorīśa and Vyādhibhakna). The others are Candragarbha and Vijñāna, followed by Tumburu who is the Bhairava of the Vāma Tantras and Amrteśvara, the Bhairava of the Netratantra. In this list of Tantras the Mālinīvijaya, which is said to have been ‘created first of all’ (68/126cd), marks, it seems, a point of entry into the higher, Kaula Tantras. The Mālinīmata is listed amongst the sixteen Mata Tantras (27-32ab) which, are all dedicated to goddesses (or to be more precise, Yoginīs) and may be considered to be Kaula. Note that the Kula of the Mālinīvijaya is here accurately identified as Trika. Beyond are the Kaula scriptures of the goddess Kubjikā of whom Klinnā is a common form (see intro. vol. 2, p. 226 ff.). While Klinnā is sometimes related to just one Krama out of the three, the Vīrāvalīkula, also called the Vīrāvalīkarma, is said to be related to the ‘fourth lineage’ which is common to all the other three (see 69/9cd-10ab). The Kālikākrama that comes next also comes after the eleventh Void associated with the Vīrāvalī as it does in the group of six associated with Parā (68/114cd-116ab). 65. Cf. above 68/91.

english: NOTES OF THE TRANSLATION OF CHAPTER SIXTY-NINE 1. Cf. above, 5/44. 2. Prabhava is the name of the first or thirty-fifth year in a sixty years’ cycle of Jupiter. 3. Pramoda is the name of the fourth year in a sixty years’ cycle of Jupiter. 4. Below ±an˜hanātha is associated, as usual, with PūrSagiri and the Dvāpara Age (69/19). 5. Nandirudra is also mentioned above in 67/8. 9. Concerning Kucandra as Kubjikā's consort and the etymology of his name, see above 7/34-35ab. According to 7/53 above, the goddess emerges out of him in the form of the Moon. She is the Transmental which is the next and last in the series of the energies of Sound. She is the will that is above the Equal One. Thus, although the goddess, as the will of the god, is commonly represented as emerging from him, here he is said to emerge from her. Moreover, here he is implictly said to be the male equivalent of the Transmental — the energy that is said to ‘emerge from the Equal One’. 13. This is another name for the OÆÆiyāna. See YKh notes p. 62. 6. Cf. above, 68/114cd-116ab, 69/4-5. The Vīrāvalīkarma is also called Vīrāvalīkula. 7. Knaya is the name of the last year of the cycle of sixty years of the planet Jupiter. 8. YKh (2) (30/44cd): At the end of the Age all the three lineages are certainly in the Li‰ga. li‰ga olyātrayaˆ [kh: -olyatrayaˆ] sarvaˆ yugānte nātra saˆśayaƒ || 10. The name of the Siddha in Kāmarūpa is Mitranātha whose name is derived from the ‘friendship’ he enjoys with the goddess. See above 4/50. 11. YKh (2) (30/49ab): He resides in Kāmarūpa and gives worldly benefits and liberation to the twice-born. kāmarūpe sthitaƒ [k: sthita; kh: (?)] so [kh: (?)] hi dvijānāˆ [k: dvijanāˆ] bhuktimuktidaƒ [k, kh: -da] | 12. Although all the MSs read ‘guÆanāthaƒ’ I have chosen the reading in YKh (2) as this is in consonance with 69/4 where it says that the Lord of this Age is OÆÆīśa. 14. Below (69/23cd) we were told that Kucandraśekhara descended onto the Island of the Moon. This, then, is the sacred seat of the Moon. By adding him to the five Siddhas, we get a set of six Siddhas and six corresponding seats. Kucandraśekhara is all five of the Siddhas, although he is also accompanied by them.
